children: Anthropic invited retail investors to participate in its historic IPO, but most retail traders faced the brick wall of geo and eligibility restrictions, becoming the exit liquidity for the opening pop.
Anthropic sold 980 million Class A shares at $83 each before trading began under the ANT ticker on 19 November.

The company allocated 15% of the offering to retail accounts, but eventually millions of self-directed traders across excluded jurisdictions and brokerages were forced to wait for Nasdaq’s opening bell.
Those secondary-market buyers entered as the stock opened 34% higher at $111.50, only to absorb an immediate 13% intraday drawdown as shares faded to close at $97.17.
Retail Investors Were Geo-fenced and Condition-Fenced
Several brokers, including Charles Schwab, Fidelity, Robinhood, Trade-PMR, SoFi and Morgan Stanley’s E*TRADE allowed retail clients to participate in Anthropic's initial offering.
However, having an account with a participating broker was not enough to qualify as an IPO investor, as many set blocking conditions.
Thus, at Fidelity, eligible traders should have at least $25,000 in certain assets and subscribe for a minimum of 25 shares - $2,075 at $83 a share.

@Maximo8136151 That's correct. Brokerage clients with at least $25,000 in eligible assets can participate in this initial public offering (IPO). If you have any other questions, don't hesitate to let us know!

Hargreaves Lansdown took applications from eligible UK clients from day one, with a minimum of £250. 45,811 applications were received with an average application of £6,661. Demand was so strong that clients ended up with 33.6% of the shares they requested.
Geo restrictions also applied: the prospectus covered retail investors from the UK, Switzerland, Australia, Canada, Japan and selected EU countries.
Secondary Buyers Absorbed the Post-Open Slide

Activity in the Czech Republic shows how retail investors have reacted in a market excluded from Anthropic's core offering. It also illustrates the prices and risks they faced in getting in after exchange trading began.
Clients of Patria, Fio and XTB entered after Nasdaq trading opened, immediately facing a price 34% above the IPO allocation.

Patria recorded activity from around 500 clients and turnover of approximately CZK100 million. Fio clients traded about $1.5 million, while Anthropic became XTB’s most-traded stock that Thursday, according to ITBiz.

The initial spike didn't last. Anthropic fell from $111.50 to $97.17 by the end of Thursday and traded just above $84 the following session, meaning secondary market buyers got a very different entry point than those who'd been allocated shares in the IPO.

Broader US trading data confirms that the first-day frenzy was driven by intense two-way flipping rather than buy-and-hold accumulation. Total retail turnover - both buy and sell orders - reached an estimated $700 million to $800 million on debut day, according to Vanda Research strategist Viraj Patel, as cited by Bloomberg.
That surpassed SpaceX’s $669 million debut earlier this year to mark the largest single-day retail IPO turnover in Vanda’s dataset dating back to 2012.

Yet net retail buying finished Thursday at roughly $60 million, half of SpaceX’s $118 million net inflow and well below Coinbase’s $92 million debut in 2021, as early holders and day-traders aggressively sold into the $111.50 opening pop while secondary buyers stepped in on the other side.
Pre-IPO CFDs Offered Only Exposure
Several brokers, including Pepperstone, EBC Financial Group, Exness, IC Markets, NAGA, and PU Prime, as well as XTB in select regions, offered pre-IPO CFDs on Anthropic.

Those instruments allowed clients to speculate on indicative valuations before the listing. Clients didn't own any Anthropic shares, didn't have any shareholder rights and didn't get any of the $83 primary allocation price.
The positions were subject to leverage, financing charges, and platform-specific repricing rules once official Nasdaq trading went live.
Anthropic's listing showed that even an estimated $12 billion retail tranche isn't enough to flatten the structural hierarchy of a blockbuster IPO.
Between the various wealth thresholds, the oversubscription rationing and the regional carve-outs, primary access was still a very privileged thing.
The rest of the retail market were simply left with the choice of either paying the $111.50 to get in at the opening peak or trading the synthetic alternatives off the sidelines.

title: Anthropic’s Two-Tier Debut: Who Got $83 Shares and Who Financed the $111.50 Open
